ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: Engineers at Columbia University have developed a synthetic muscle that can be used for humanoid robots and can imitate human muscles to perform actions such as pushing, pulling, bending, and twisting. As shown in the figure, one end of a sufficiently long thin rope ab connected to an object of mass m is fixed to the wall; the d end of the “arm” ced made of synthetic muscle is fixed with a pulley, and the c end is fixed to the wall. The thin rope passes around the pulley. c and e are similar to joints of a human arm and are controlled by the synthetic muscle of the “arm.” Let the angle between cd and the vertical wall ac be $\theta$. Neglecting the friction between the pulley and the thin rope, which of the following statements is correct ( )
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text: If ac is kept equal to ad and the length of cd is increased, the force of the thin rope on the pulley is always along the dc direction

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: on the left side of the figure is a vertical wall; point a is above and point c is below, and ac is a vertical line segment; at point d on the right side a pulley is fixed. One section of the thin rope connects obliquely downward from point a on the wall to the pulley d, and after passing around the pulley, the other section connects vertically downward from d to the heavy object b. In the figure there is also an “arm” support rod from c through e to d, and d is to the upper right of c. Then reason: the pulley and the thin rope have no friction, so the tensions in the two sections of the rope have the same magnitude, denoted T. The two forces of the thin rope on the pulley are respectively along the d→a direction and along the d→b vertically downward direction. Keep ac=ad, let ac=ad=L, take c as the origin, the vertically upward direction as the y-axis, and the horizontally rightward direction as the x-axis, then a=(0,L), d=(x,y), and ad=L. The unit direction along d→a is ((-x),(L-y))/L, and the unit direction along d→b is (0,-1). Therefore the direction of the resultant force is proportional to ((-x)/L,(L-y)/L-1)=((-x)/L,(-y)/L), which is parallel to the vector d→c=(-x,-y). Therefore, no matter how the length of cd is increased, as long as ac=ad is kept, the direction of the resultant force of the thin rope on the pulley is always along the dc direction.
